pr_title: cquery: support queries over incompatible targets.
pr_body:
The implementation is a simple matter of adding an extra "should we report incompatible errors?" bit to the build request. Keep it true on builds, false on cquery.

Fixes https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/13861.
pr_comments: @philsc I'd love your review too (but I can't assign to you).

So what `cquery` is going to do with the incompatible targets - remove them from the output or keep them in the output? It looks like this change prevents `cquery` from failing when it hits incompatible target, but still outputs that target. Is that right? We really need a way to skip incompatible targets from the output. May be we can have a flag for that?
@konste , you can filter out incompatible targets like so: https://docs.bazel.build/versions/main/platforms.html#detecting-incompatible-targets-using-bazel-cquery

I agree with @philsc .

There are contradictory needs here. One need is as you describe: identifying and skipping incompatible targets. The other need is to be able to identify them in the first place, including where they appear in the dependency graph and how the build gets to them. 

I don't think cquery should be in the business of worrying about the distinction between incompatible vs. compatible targets. What it should do is not fail, which is what this PR handles. For those who want to specially identify incompatible targets I'd hope the right specific query would be the way to do that, as @philsc links.

Is that workable for you?

@philsc yes, this is what we do right now. But it looks... bulky? Also every time incompatible target is skipped from `cquery` output it is replaced with the empty line, which makes processing the output more cumbersome. But all inconveniences aside - yes, it does the job.

@gregestren if it is not too much work I would like to have a flag which skips incompatible targets from `cquery` output OR alternatively mark them somehow in the output so they can be skipped by the following code. But I admit it is just the convenience thing and not a blocker.

I don't think anyone wants cquery to actually error on incompatible targets, so I think his PR is a pure improvement regardless of how we address your concerns.

In that spirit, can we consider the issues separately? i.e. submit this PR as-is and file a separate issue for your concerns that we'll consider independently?

For reasons described we're really reluctant to bake in too much specific functionality, especially when there are reasonable alternatives through Starlark, where we try to route as much user customization power as we can. I'd remain really resistant to a cquery flag. One of the goals of cquery's Starlark output was to save us from creating new output formatters (`--output=...`) for the myriad ways users want to consume the output.

But I am more open to the idea of somehow annotating the output. i.e. cquery results already show configuration hashes and whether they're in the HOST configuration. Adding a `(incompatible)` suffix could be consistent. I don't want to guarantee that without further discussion, but that's where I'd focus the feature request.
@katre I think I'm ready for your code owner review.
Yes @gregestren I agree that this PR is a pure improvement and should go forward regardless. I will open a separate feature request for annotating incompatible `cquery` outputs.

issue_context.title: Bazel cquery fails if paths are incompatible for platform
issue_context.body:
### Description of the problem / feature request:

Bazel `cquery` is a useful command for finding build dependencies you wish to avoid/remove in a specific configuration.

If you use Bazel `cquery` to find `somepath` or `allpaths` to a incompatible target, it will error with:

```
bazel --nohome_rc cquery  'allpaths(//foo:bar, //foo:baz)'
```
```
ERROR: Target //foo:baz is incompatible and cannot be built, but was explicitly requested.
```

As this is failing in a `bazel build` step, it actually does produce a relevant result, but accidentally, and if there are no query results, it simply returns an error instead of 0 results.

### Bugs: what's the simplest, easiest way to reproduce this bug? Please provide a minimal example if possible.

Using the following trivial `BUILD.bazel`, with one incompatible target:
```
sh_test(
    name = "foo",
    srcs = ["BUILD.bazel"],
)

sh_test(
    name = "bar",
    srcs = ["BUILD.bazel"],
)

sh_test(
    name = "baz",
    srcs = ["BUILD.bazel"],
    target_compatible_with = ["@platforms//:incompatible"],
)
```

A `cquery` between the targets shows how `cquery` will `ERROR` if the target is an incompatible target.
```
$ bazel cquery 'somepath(:foo, :bar)'
INFO: Analyzed 2 targets (1 packages loaded, 430 targets configured).
INFO: Found 2 targets...
INFO: Empty query results
INFO: Elapsed time: 0.770s
INFO: 0 processes.
INFO: Build completed successfully, 0 total actions
$ bazel cquery 'somepath(:foo, :baz)'
ERROR: Target //:baz is incompatible and cannot be built, but was explicitly requested.
Dependency chain:
    //:baz   <-- target platform didn't satisfy constraint @platforms//:incompatible
INFO: Elapsed time: 0.243s
INFO: 0 processes.
FAILED: Build did NOT complete successfully (0 packages loaded, 3 targets configured)
```

Repeating the same command with `bazel query`:
```
$ bazel query 'somepath(:foo, :baz)'
INFO: Empty results
$ bazel query 'somepath(:foo, :bar)'
INFO: Empty results
Loading: 0 packages loaded
```

### What operating system are you running Bazel on?

Ubuntu 18.04

### What's the output of `bazel info release`?

`release 4.1.0`

###  Have you found anything relevant by searching the web?

No

The closest issue I can find is #13019, which is a separate query/genquery issue.
comments:
Interesting. what output are you hoping for? A full result with no errors?

Due to how incompatible target skipping is implemented, I suspect this is a design limitation. i.e. `cquery` literally starts an actual build. When incompatible target skipping kicks in it returns that error before cquery has a chance to look at the dep graph.

FYI @philsc.

In an ideal world, I was hoping that `bazel cquery` works regardless of whether or not the code is actually build-able, since my main reasons for using the command are fixing or avoiding build issues. I need `cquery` instead of `query` as `select()` statements usually divert the incompatible dependencies. This is a corner case that interrupts normal bazel graph debugging workflows.

I found this because:

 1. Build error in our build due to dependency on incompatible target
 2. Try to use `bazel cquery` to find places where this incompatible target is leaking in
 3. Realize that `bazel cquery` isn't actually working, but able to keep debugging with just `bazel build` commands

The error output gives me similar information; however, it provides that information as error output, it only mimics `somepath`-like queries, and it always has an error result, which makes it difficult to use the command in automated tooling. 

I filed this bug after discussing this with @philsc in the hopes that there is some way of addressing this behavior longer term. That said, this is not super critical.

This is fair. Conceptually cquery doesn't need to do *complete* analysis like in a real build. i.e. it doesn't actually need to create actions.

@katre and I have tossed around the idea of having `cquery` do more limited processing that avoids that. That would relieve this problem and reduce cases where `cquery`  doesn't work as a debugging tool because it fails just like the real build. We've noticed that annoyance too.

Less ambitiously, we could try having `cquery` make all targets "implicit". Incompatible target skipping, by its very name, is capable of skipping targets instead of failing, so long as you're building `:all`. I'm not sure what the code that flips that bit would look like.

I'm also curious what happens if you add [`--keep_going`](https://docs.bazel.build/versions/main/user-manual.html#flag--keep_going) to your query. I really have no idea if that helps, but it's an interesting interaction.

I think it makes sense for `cquery` to run these kinds of queries. The error that's currently being printed is really only meaningful when the user tries to build the target (since it's impossible to build an incompatible target).

At this time with Bazel 4.2.1 I observe that `cquery` returns incompatible targets as well as compatible and this actually creates a problem for us, because we feed `cquery` output to the following `build` and it fails with `Target ... is incompatible and cannot be built, but was explicitly requested.`
Is there a way to make cquery skip incompatible targets?
Otherwise is there a way to query for incompatible targets in order to remove those from the results of the first query?
<15 min later>
I have found https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/12917 and it seems to answer my questions.

Happy you got a resolution, @konste . :)

Following up on my last comment, for the original bug, can anyone verify if adding `--keep_going` to the `cquery` gets around this? I'm specifically interested because of 

https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/blob/33f7648fbaa875f73416be47f0b3c10ed93f30d6/src/main/java/com/google/devtools/build/lib/analysis/constraints/TopLevelConstraintSemantics.java#L146-L164

which implies `--keep_going` demotes the error to a warning.

All - I put up https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/pull/14311 to try to address this issue.

I'm very interested in your feedback. It's a bit of a paradigm shift for cquery and could introduce its own confusion (i.e. what @konste reported two comments above). But I'm cautiously optimistic this paradigm would be more sustainable.

review_comments:
I admittedly don't know anything about the Java style guide, but this seems more readable as `request.incompatibleTargetsShouldBeReported()`. Though obviously more wordy. Otherwise, it makes it seem like this function actually reports targets and returns success/failure of the report maybe? Not sure. Basically phrase it like an assertion.

Anyway, just a stream of consciousness that I had. I guess I should read up on the Java style guide.

EDIT: looking at all the other booleans in this code, looks like this is being consistent. So nevermind!
